sub_questions.question: Using the UN FAO SOFI 2023 and 2024 reports, explain how rising food prices affect food security, including impacts on hunger, food insecurity, malnutrition, and the main drivers and vulnerable groups.

route.reason: The request is about the impact of price increases on food security, which falls squarely within the FAO SOFI sustainability and food-security evidence base.

csr.question: Using the UN FAO SOFI 2023 and 2024 reports, explain how rising food prices affect food security, including impacts on hunger, food insecurity, malnutrition, and the main drivers and vulnerable groups.

answer.summary: SOFI 2023 and 2024 describe rising food prices as a major transmission channel through which conflict, climate shocks, economic slowdowns, energy/input costs and trade disruptions reduce access to food and healthy diets. The result is higher hunger and food insecurity, poorer diet quality, and greater risk of malnutrition, especially where inflation combines with inequality, import dependence, conflict or climate extremes. Confirmed report findings are separated below from implications for corporate action.

findings.claim: In SOFI 2023, rising prices of food, agricultural inputs and energy—magnified by the war in Ukraine—undermined food security in 2022; 691–783 million people faced hunger in 2022, with a midrange of about 735 million, or 122 million more than in 2019 before the pandemic.

SOFI 2023 links high food, fuel and transport prices after the pandemic to stalled progress on food security; in 2022, Asia accounted for about 55% of undernourished people, Africa about 38% or 282 million, and Latin America and the Caribbean about 6% or 43 million.

Food price inflation affects food security mainly by reducing economic access: households with limited income face higher costs for basic food and nutritious diets, while producers may also face higher input and energy costs, limiting supply responses.

SOFI 2023 identifies conflict, climate variability and extremes, economic slowdowns/downturns and inequality as major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition; price shocks often interact with these drivers rather than acting alone.

Regional impacts differ. In Southern Africa, the 2022 rise in hunger was linked to inflation after international commodity price increases, unemployment and vulnerability to shocks; in Western Asia, political instability and conflict disrupted supplies and markets, causing higher prices and shortages; in the Caribbean, import dependence exposed small island states to high food inflation and import bills.

SOFI 2024 confirms that the world remains off track on SDG Targets 2.1 and 2.2, with persistently high hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition driven by conflict, climate extremes and economic slowdowns, combined with lack of access to and unaffordability of healthy diets, unhealthy food environments and persistent inequality.

Malnutrition impacts arise because high prices and unaffordable healthy diets push households toward cheaper, less diverse and less nutritious foods, while compounding shocks affect care practices, health services, water and sanitation, and child and maternal nutrition determinants.

Vulnerable groups highlighted in SOFI 2024 include rural populations, where extreme poverty and food insecurity remain deeply entrenched, and women, youth and Indigenous Peoples, who are disproportionately affected.

recommendations.action: Prioritize affordability of nutritious foods in CSR programmes, e.g., targeted food vouchers, healthy school meals, maternal/child nutrition support or subsidies for nutrient-dense foods.
recommendations.why: This addresses the driver of unaffordable healthy diets and food price inflation. Impact can be tracked through household food insecurity, diet diversity and affordability of a healthy diet indicators.

recommendations.action: Support smallholder and local food supply resilience through input access, climate-smart agronomy, storage, logistics and market-linkage investments.
recommendations.why: Higher input, energy and transport costs amplify food price shocks; strengthening local production and supply chains can reduce vulnerability to disruptions and improve availability of nutritious foods.

recommendations.action: Design programmes specifically for high-risk geographies: conflict-affected markets, climate-exposed rural areas, import-dependent small island states and inflation-hit urban/peri-urban communities.
recommendations.why: SOFI shows price impacts vary by region and are worst when combined with conflict, climate extremes, import dependence or weak livelihoods.

recommendations.action: Embed gender, youth and Indigenous Peoples targeting in food security investments.
recommendations.why: SOFI 2024 identifies these populations as disproportionately affected, so targeting improves equity and the likelihood of measurable nutrition impact.

recommendations.action: Use a resilience-financing lens: combine short-term food assistance with longer-term investments in livelihoods, climate adaptation and peace-sensitive market recovery.
recommendations.why: SOFI 2024 calls for financing aligned to drivers including conflict, climate extremes and economic shocks, and for linking humanitarian and development approaches.

next_steps: Map company operations and sourcing regions against food price inflation, conflict, climate and import-dependence risks.
Identify affected stakeholder groups: workers, smallholder suppliers, surrounding communities, women, youth and Indigenous Peoples.
Choose 2–3 priority intervention areas where the company has leverage: wages/livelihoods, food access, supply-chain resilience or nutrition.
Set a baseline using food security and nutrition indicators before programme launch.
Partner with local governments, WFP/FAO/UNICEF actors, NGOs or producer organizations to avoid duplicating existing interventions.
Report outcomes annually using SOFI-aligned indicators and disaggregate by gender, age, location and livelihood group.

kpis.metric: Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity using FIES
kpis.how_to_measure: Survey beneficiary households before and after intervention using the Food Insecurity Experience Scale.
Track local cost of a healthy diet against household income or wages in target communities.

kpis.metric: Household dietary diversity or minimum dietary diversity for women/children
kpis.how_to_measure: Use 24-hour recall surveys to assess whether higher prices are reducing consumption of nutritious food groups.
Where appropriate and ethically managed, monitor stunting, wasting or minimum acceptable diet through health or nutrition partners.

kpis.metric: Price and supply stability for nutritious foods
kpis.how_to_measure: Monitor market prices, stockouts and transport/logistics disruptions for priority nutritious foods in intervention areas.

risks_assumptions: Food price interventions can distort local markets if poorly targeted or not coordinated with public systems.
Nutrition outcomes require more than food access; health, WASH, care practices and gender dynamics also matter.
Conflict and climate shocks may overwhelm company-level interventions without public and humanitarian coordination.
The answer uses SOFI 2023 figures for 2022 hunger and SOFI 2024 for the financing/drivers framing; figures are not mixed without year context.

At the regional level, this dynamic of income and price effect is visible in multiple subregions, with varying results. In Southern Africa , for instance, the uptick of hunger in 2022 stemmed from increasing inflation, following the upsurge in international commodity prices, as well as domestic challenges such as persistently high levels of unemployment and vulnerability to shocks. 11 Although there was sustained GDP growth in 2022, this often did not translate into improved socioeconomic conditions for the poor. sources.title: FAO SOFI 2023: The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World
sources.text: FOREWORD This report brings our organizations together again to reaffirm that, if we do not redouble and better target our efforts, our goal of ending hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition in all its forms by 2030 will remain out of reach. Although the world is recovering from the global pandemic, this is occurring unevenly across and within countries. On top of this, the world is grappling with the consequences of the ongoing war in Ukraine, which has shaken food and energy markets. Agrifood systems remain highly vulnerable to shocks and disruptions arising from conflict, climate variability and extremes, and economic contraction. These factors, combined with growing inequities, keep challenging the capacity of agrifood systems to deliver nutritious, safe and affordable diets for all. These major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition are our “new normal”. We have no option but to redouble our efforts to transform agrifood systems and leverage them towards reaching the Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG 2) targets. Global hunger is still far above pre-pandemic levels. It is estimated that between 690 and 783 million people in the world faced hunger in 2022. This is 122 million more people than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Economic recovery hampered by new challenges to food security At the end of 2021, global food security was on high alert due to lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic as well as new and ongoing conflicts and weather-related shocks. A combination of an unequal economic recovery after a dramatic decrease in economic activity observed in 2020, and rising food, fuel and transportation prices produced by the recovery itself, thwarted progress in food security. Just as global economic conditions appeared to be more favourable for 2022 and the prospects of a reduction in hunger and food insecurity towards pre-pandemic levels seemed possible, the outbreak of the war in Ukraine sent another shock through the global economy.

sources.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The reverse in progress and the persistently high levels of hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition in recent years have put the world off track to meet Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Targets 2.1 and 2.2 – to end hunger, food insecurity and all forms of malnutrition by 2030. Previous editions of this report have repeatedly highlighted the intensification of several major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition, specifically conflict, climate variability and extremes, and economic slowdowns and downturns, combined with the well-established underlying factors that contribute to food insecurity and malnutrition, such as lack of access to and unaffordability of healthy diets, unhealthy food environments, and high and persistent inequality. Not only are these major drivers increasing in frequency and intensity, they are occurring concurrently more often, and in combination with the underlying factors, resulting in increasing numbers of hungry and food-insecure people. Depending on the major driver or combination of drivers affecting food security and nutrition in a country, addressing them will require a portfolio of policies across six transformative pathways, as outlined in detail in The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2021.

sources.text: THE STATE OF FOOD SECURITY AND NUTRITION IN THE WORLD 2024 The high proportion of countries affected by at least one major driver builds the case for mainstreaming food security and nutrition objectives across other sector financing where the priorities do not always include meeting SDG Targets 2.1 and 2.2. Considering that climate extremes are the most prevalent driver in all country groups, the opportunity of creating synergies between food security and nutrition and climate objectives will be essential for scaling up enough resources to fill the funding gap. On the other hand, the relevance of conflict as a driver in countries with limited access to financing calls for strengthening the humanitarian–development–peace nexus, as well as for bridging the short ‑term horizon of humanitarian operations with the needed long‑term perspective of investments oriented to eradicating hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition. In addition, the higher PoU and stunting levels found in countries with limited or moderate access to financing emphasize the urgency of scaling up financing flows for ending hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition.

Financing therefore encompasses all the interventions aligned with the six transformative policy pathways designed to strengthen the resilience of agrifood systems to the major drivers behind hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition – namely conflict, climate variability and extremes, and economic slowdowns and downturns – and address the underlying structural factors: lack of access to and unaffordability of nutritious foods, unhealthy food environments, and high and persistent inequality. To generate a framework for increased financing and improved finance targeting, it is imperative to gain an understanding of the major drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition, and of the countries affected by these major drivers. In the last ten years, the frequency and intensity of conflict, climate extremes and economic downturns have increased, undermining food security and nutrition around the world. Furthermore, high levels of income inequality exacerbate the effects of these drivers. While each of these major drivers is unique, they often interact to create multiple compounding impacts transmitted through agrifood systems to the detriment of food security and nutrition.

sources.title: FAO SOFI 2024: The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World
sources.text: FOREWORD Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is the responsibility of all countries. Our five organizations support transformative efforts to progress towards a world free from hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition in all its forms by 2030. We are encouraged by the commitment of national governments, partners all over the world and the global community towards this common goal. While we have made some progress, improvements have been uneven and insufficient. We have seen improvement in more populous countries with growing economies, but hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition continue to increase in many countries around the world. This is affecting millions of people especially in rural areas, where extreme poverty and food insecurity remain deeply entrenched. Vulnerable populations, particularly women, youth and Indigenous Peoples, are disproportionately affected. A continuation of the past trends means that by 2030, millions of people will still be undernourished, millions of children will still be affected by malnutrition in its different forms, and the world will still be falling short of reaching the global nutrition targets.
